name: Familial encephalopathy with neuroserpin inclusion bodies (FENIB)
aliases: familial encephalopathy with neuroserpin inclusion bodies

reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the neuroserpin gene (SERPINI1), belonging to the serpinopathies (conformational protein-polymerisation diseases)
Presents with progressive dementia and, in many patients, myoclonus and seizures, with the age of onset and severity linked to the specific mutation
Pathology shows characteristic neuronal intracytoplasmic inclusions, called Collins bodies, composed of polymerised mutant neuroserpin
More disruptive mutations generally produce earlier onset and more severe disease, illustrating a genotype-phenotype correlation
The mechanism parallels other serpinopathies such as alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, in which mutant serpin molecules polymerise and are retained within cells
A family history of early dementia with myoclonus or epilepsy should raise suspicion
Diagnosis rests on the clinical picture, family history, SERPINI1 genetic testing and, where available, characteristic pathology
reference.pathophysiology: Familial encephalopathy with neuroserpin inclusion bodies is an autosomal dominant serpinopathy caused by mutations in SERPINI1, the gene encoding neuroserpin, a serine protease inhibitor secreted by neurones. The mutant protein is prone to aberrant conformational change and polymerisation, so that molecules link together and are retained within the endoplasmic reticulum of neurones, forming intracytoplasmic inclusions known as Collins bodies. The resulting protein overload and neuronal dysfunction cause progressive encephalopathy; the extent of polymerisation and inclusion burden, determined by the particular mutation, correlates with the age of onset and disease severity, ranging from a later-onset dementia to an early, severe encephalopathy with epilepsy.
additionalDifferentials: Progressive myoclonic epilepsies of other cause
Alzheimer disease and other early-onset dementias
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and other prion diseases
Lafora disease and neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses
additionalInvestigations: SERPINI1 gene testing to confirm the diagnosis
MRI of the brain to assess atrophy and exclude alternative pathology
Electroencephalography to characterise epileptic and myoclonic activity
Neuropsychological assessment to document the cognitive decline
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis to help exclude inflammatory, infective and prion causes
Neuropathological examination demonstrating neuroserpin inclusions where available
redFlags: Frequent or poorly controlled seizures and disabling myoclonus
Rapidly progressive encephalopathy, particularly with early-onset mutations
Cognitive decline compromising safety and capacity
Family history indicating dominant inheritance with implications for relatives
reference.prognosis: The disorder is progressive, and prognosis depends strongly on the mutation, with earlier-onset forms causing severe encephalopathy and epilepsy and later-onset forms a slower dementia; management is supportive, including seizure and myoclonus control and genetic counselling.
pitfalls: Not considering a serpinopathy in a familial dementia accompanied by myoclonus or epilepsy
Confusing the presentation with prion disease or other progressive myoclonic epilepsies without genetic testing
Overlooking the genotype-phenotype correlation when counselling about prognosis
Failing to offer genetic counselling to at-risk relatives given the dominant inheritance
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
